traditions.title: Traditional Thai Food and Regional Food Culture
traditions.description: How do the staples and seasonings of Central, Northern, Isan and Southern Thailand differ? Learn about signature dishes, regional flavors and what to know before you order for the first time.
traditions.eyebrow: Traditional Thai food and food culture
traditions.h1: Within one country,|the way people eat and the flavors change
traditions.intro: If you have tried Pad Thai and Tom Yum Goong, there is much more Thai food to discover. In Chiang Mai you eat sticky rice with sausage, vegetables and dipping sauce, while in Isan people enjoy crunchy papaya salad and tangy fermented foods. Some dishes, like the noodles and snacks of Phuket, are specific to a city. Just as you might compare barbecue styles from region to region in the US, look for something new in the city you are visiting.
traditions.note: If Thai food is new to you, start with **a bowl of curry or noodles with rice**. With friends or family, order several dishes to share and try different flavors.
basics: In the Central region, meals are built around steamed rice with several dishes, while the North and Isan often eat sticky rice. Noodle dishes differ by region too.
Chilies, herbs, sour ingredients, fish sauce and fermented ingredients are combined depending on the dish. The flavor makers are different from dish to dish.
This guide introduces the main traits of the Central, Northern, Northeastern (Isan) and Southern regions. Even within a region, the food of each city and community differs.
Check **the ingredients in seasonings and sauces** too. You cannot tell from the name of a vegetable or chicken dish whether it is vegetarian or halal.
traditions.regionsH2: Looking at it region by region shows the flavors more clearly
traditions.orderH2: How to choose when you order for the first time
order: First decide whether you want to share rice with several dishes or have one bowl of noodles.
Pick the meat, fish or shrimp you want, and tell the staff about anything you avoid, including seasonings.
**Ask about spice level before you order.** Broth or sauce that is already made may be hard to adjust.
When the food arrives, taste it first, then add extra seasoning and condiments a little at a time.
faq: Is all Thai food spicy?
Desserts and some dishes are not meant to be spicy. For curries and dipping sauces, you cannot judge the heat from the color or name, so it helps to ask before you order.
Do you only eat a regional specialty in that region?
Many dishes have spread and are eaten across the country. This guide explains links to regional food culture and does not claim a place of origin or an exclusive area.
Is a dish with vegetables vegetarian?
Some dishes use animal-based seasonings such as fish sauce and shrimp paste. If you have a dietary restriction, ask the staff to tell you the actual ingredients, including seasonings.

order: For roti, compare the price of the plain version with versions that add toppings such as banana or egg.

Look at the stall's menu and posted prices and order only what you need. Do not assume the same name means the same price or ingredients.

fruitPrices.compareH2: How to compare on the same price tag
compare: Compare the same variety, size and grade. For thick-skinned fruit such as durian, ask whether the kilogram price includes the husk or is for the flesh only.

Check how much flesh goes into one bag or one pack. It is not the same as the weight of whole fruit with its peel.
Cup size, ingredients, and how ice and syrup are used all differ. Do not compare the per-kilogram price of watermelon with a cup of watermelon shake as if they were the same product.

central.name: Central Thailand
central.subtitle: The Central table, where curry goes with rice
central.text: In Central Thailand, curries and several other dishes are eaten with steamed rice. The richness of coconut milk, sour, sweet and spicy notes come together differently in each dish. If you eat Tom Yum Goong and green curry in Bangkok, you can taste this combination of flavors.

north.name: Northern Thailand
north.subtitle: The North, where sticky rice and vegetables come with dipping sauce
north.text: In the North, sticky rice and vegetables are eaten with nam prik, and the herb-scented sausage sai ua is a favorite. Khao soi in Chiang Mai puts noodles and curry broth in one bowl. Not all Northern food is mild, so ask about the spice level when you order.

isan.name: Northeastern Thailand (Isan)
isan.subtitle: Isan, with crunchy papaya and tangy fermented food
isan.text: In Isan, try som tam and larb with sticky rice. Some dishes use pla ra, a fermented fish seasoning. Even within Isan, som tam differs in the chilies and seasonings used, so you can enjoy a different flavor from place to place.

south.name: Southern Thailand
south.subtitle: The South, where seafood, noodles and many cultures meet
south.text: In the South you can enjoy spicy dishes, and also noodles and snacks that differ by city. Phuket has dishes shaped by Chinese and Malay food culture, and the Songkhla area has the food of Chinese and Muslim communities side by side. Pick the city you are visiting and explore its signature dishes.

bangkok.name: Bangkok
bangkok.tag: Where flavors from across Thailand meet
bangkok.intro: If you are choosing your first meal in Bangkok, start with Pad Thai. At the next meal, try a curry with rice or share a pot of Tom Yum Goong. Finish with mango sticky rice for something sweet. In Bangkok you will find Central Thai food and dishes from many other regions of Thailand too.
bangkok.culture: Bangkok is a city where the food of many Thai regions comes together. The choices run from Central Thai rice and curries to dishes that came from other regions. This guide introduces signature dishes that are easy to pick even if Bangkok is your first taste of Thai food.
bangkok.note: The dishes below are not local specialties eaten only in Bangkok. You can find them in many cities across Thailand.
bangkok.pairing: If you are eating alone, pick a plate of Pad Thai or a curry with rice. With friends or family, share Tom Yum Goong and finish with a plate of mango sticky rice for dessert.
bangkok.priceGuide: In Bangkok, keep the per-kilogram price of whole fruit separate from the price of a pack of cut fruit. Below are official retail prices by variety and grade surveyed on the same day. They can differ from what an individual stall charges at a tourist spot.

chiang-mai.name: Chiang Mai
chiang-mai.tag: Lanna aromas and sticky rice culture
chiang-mai.intro: In Chiang Mai, start your Northern Thai meals with a bowl of khao soi. You get soft noodles, crispy noodles and a rich curry broth together. At the next meal, try herb-scented sai ua and the tomato-based dip nam prik ong with sticky rice. You will see a Northern table that is quite different from a noodle dish.
chiang-mai.culture: In the North, sticky rice is eaten with several side dishes, vegetables and nam prik. The khantoke meal, with food set out on small tables, shows this food culture as well. Khantoke is not the name of one dish. It refers to the tray of many dishes and the way of sharing the meal.
chiang-mai.note: Khao soi, sai ua and nam prik ong are eaten not only in Chiang Mai but in other parts of the North too.
chiang-mai.pairing: If you want a simple lunch, pick khao soi. On a day when you are sharing several dishes, order sai ua and nam prik ong with sticky rice and vegetables for a full Northern Thai meal.
chiang-mai.priceGuide: In Chiang Mai, look at longan and lychee, which are linked to the North. For fruit sold in bunches, ask whether the weight includes the stems. Treat dried longan and fresh fruit as separate products with their own package weights.

phuket.name: Phuket
phuket.tag: Noodles and snacks shaped by Chinese and Malay culture
phuket.intro: In Phuket, you do not have to stop at grilled seafood. Try mi hokkien, a stir-fry of thick noodles, and mi hun, made with thin rice noodles. After the meal, take a break with o-aew, a cup of ice and jelly. Add the local food to a day of exploring Old Phuket Town.
phuket.culture: The food of Phuket carries the influence of Chinese and Malay food culture. Thick noodles may be stir-fried with seafood, and thin noodles may come with a pork rib broth. Once you look at snacks made with ice and jelly too, the Phuket table you thought of as seafood looks much more varied.
phuket.note: Mi hokkien and mi hun are different noodle dishes. If you order them by name, you can enjoy the difference in noodle texture and in what comes with each.
phuket.pairing: For a meal, have mi hokkien or mi hun, and on a hot day pick o-aew for dessert. If you are with a group, share both noodle dishes and compare thick and thin noodles.
phuket.priceGuide: In Phuket, keep cut fruit or drinks you eat right on the beach separate from whole fruit. If you convert the price of one bag or one cup into a per-kilogram price to compare, the amount you actually eat can be very different.

ayutthaya.name: Ayutthaya
ayutthaya.tag: River food and roti sai mai
ayutthaya.intro: In Ayutthaya, have boat noodles for lunch while you tour the ruins. If you want to share a meal with your group, you could pick grilled river prawns. Roti sai mai, thin roti wrapped around spun sugar, is a snack to try in Ayutthaya. Wrap one yourself and enjoy a sweet break on your trip.
ayutthaya.culture: Ayutthaya sits close to the river, and a food trip built around noodles and river prawns is well known there. You can also try roti sai mai, which Muslim communities have kept going. Eat noodles for a meal and wrap spun sugar in roti for a snack, and enjoy the different foods of the same city.
ayutthaya.note: Boat noodles are eaten in other cities too. The price of river prawns changes with size and selling unit, so look at the prawns you are ordering before you decide.
ayutthaya.pairing: Have boat noodles for lunch, and for a meal with several people, share grilled river prawns and rice. Roti sai mai is easy to wrap one sheet at a time while you adjust how much spun sugar to use.
ayutthaya.priceGuide: On a day touring the ruins in Ayutthaya, decide first how much fruit you want to eat right away. Each fruit has its own unit: bananas are sold by the bunch and whole watermelons by the kilogram. For cut fruit in a bag or pack, look at the amount and the price together.

khon-kaen.name: Khon Kaen
khon-kaen.tag: Isan fermented flavors and freshwater fish dishes
khon-kaen.intro: In Khon Kaen, enjoy Isan food with som tam and larb alongside sticky rice. Crunchy papaya, savory meat and a tangy dressing can be shared in a single meal. Also look at the fermented sausage sai krok Isan and au pla, a freshwater fish curry. Even within the same region, these dishes differ in ingredients and in how they are eaten.
khon-kaen.culture: In Isan, sticky rice and fermented seasonings are used widely. Som tam is made by pounding papaya, larb uses herbs and toasted rice powder, and a sausage ferments rice and pork, so the ways of building flavor vary. This guide also introduces au pla, a local dish of Khon Kaen that uses freshwater fish.
khon-kaen.note: Som tam, larb and sai krok Isan are eaten in many parts of Isan. Au pla is a dish introduced as a local specialty of Khon Kaen.
khon-kaen.pairing: When you eat som tam or larb, order sticky rice with it. If the aroma of fermentation is new to you, first ask whether the som tam is made with pla ra. On a day when you want fish instead of meat, look at au pla.
khon-kaen.priceGuide: In Khon Kaen, tell apart ripe papaya, which you eat as fruit, from the green papaya used in som tam. When you buy whole fruit, look at the per-kilogram price and the total weight, and for cut fruit, look at the amount in one pack.

hat-yai.name: Hat Yai
hat-yai.tag: Fried chicken and soup dishes of the Songkhla area
hat-yai.intro: In Hat Yai, try fried chicken served with fried shallots. When you eat the chicken and the shallots together, you get crispness and a savory aroma. If you want a different kind of meal, you could also pick bak kut teh, a herb-scented pork rib soup. Explore the varied food culture of the Songkhla area one dish at a time.
hat-yai.culture: The Songkhla area, where Hat Yai is located, has the food of Chinese and Muslim communities side by side. Some meals center on sticky rice and fried chicken, while others center on bak kut teh with its Chinese herb aroma. The meat and seasonings differ from dish to dish, so choose something together that everyone in your group can eat.
hat-yai.note: Bak kut teh is not presented as a dish that originated in Hat Yai. Even for a chicken dish, you cannot tell from the name of the dish whether it is halal.
hat-yai.pairing: Eat the fried chicken with sticky rice. Eat the fried shallots together with the chicken, and add the sauce a little at a time. On a day when you want a warm broth meal, pick bak kut teh, which uses pork ribs.
hat-yai.priceGuide: In Hat Yai, look at harvest periods by growing region for Southern fruit too. Even for the same rambutan or mangosteen, harvest differs by area. When you buy a single bag, ask about the weight in the bag and the total price.

pad-thai.name: Pad Thai
pad-thai.intro: If you cannot decide what to eat first in Thailand, order Pad Thai. Rice noodles are stir-fried with egg and tofu in a sweet and tangy tamarind sauce. Crunchy bean sprouts and savory peanuts give you several textures on a single plate. Squeeze the lime wedge that comes on the side and the tang really comes alive.
pad-thai.flavor: Tamarind's tang meets sweetness and salt. Eat the soft noodles together with bean sprouts and peanuts and you get a crunchy, nutty bite. At places that bring dried chili flakes on the side, you can add as much as you like.
pad-thai.ingredients: Rice noodles with egg, tofu and bean sprouts, seasoned with tamarind. Shrimp, dried shrimp and peanuts are sometimes used, so tell the staff before you order if there is anything you avoid.
pad-thai.story: Pad Thai is Thailand's best-known stir-fried noodle dish. It is easy to find in Bangkok, but it is not a local specialty eaten only there. If you are new to Thai food, start with Pad Thai, and at your next meal try a noodle dish with broth such as khao soi.
pad-thai.tip: If you cannot eat shrimp, ask whether dried shrimp and the seasoning contain it too.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as shrimp, and place your order. If you cannot eat shrimp, ask whether dried shrimp is included as well.
When the plate arrives, try it as it is first. Add the lime and peanuts a little at a time to adjust the tang and the nuttiness to your taste.
If you like heat, add a little dried chili. If you need to leave out egg or peanuts, tell the staff before the dish is made.
faq: Does Pad Thai always have shrimp?

No. The main ingredient depends on the menu item. Even when you cannot see shrimp, dried shrimp is sometimes used in the seasoning, so if you cannot eat shrimp, ask about both the main ingredient and the seasoning.
Can I only eat it in Bangkok?
No. It is a signature dish eaten in many cities across Thailand. On a trip to Bangkok, it makes a good first meal to ease into Thai food.

tom-yum-kung.name: Tom Yum Goong
tom-yum-kung.intro: Try Tom Yum Goong, a hot broth with the aroma of lemongrass and kaffir lime leaves. It is Thailand's signature soup, simmered with shrimp and made sour and spicy. One spoonful gives you tang, heat and herbs together. If you are eating with friends or family, order rice and share a bowl of Tom Yum Goong.
tom-yum-kung.flavor: Sour and spicy notes build on a broth that tastes of shrimp. Lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaves give tom yum its distinctive aroma. Some versions are clear and others are rich, so dishes with the same name can taste a little different.
tom-yum-kung.ingredients: Shrimp, with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves and more for aroma. Seasoning and broth vary with the recipe.
tom-yum-kung.story: Tom yum goong is a dish whose cooking has been passed down in households and communities. The cooking knowledge and culture around it was added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024. It is not a certification for a particular restaurant, but recognition of the culture of making and sharing food that people have handed down.
tom-yum-kung.tip: If you cannot eat shrimp, choose a different dish instead of Tom Yum Goong.
steps: Look at whether the menu offers a clear broth or a rich one, and choose. If you want less heat, say so when you order. Broth that is already simmered may be hard to adjust.
Sip the broth a little at a time with rice. If you are with a group, ladle it into individual bowls and share the shrimp and broth.
The tough lemongrass stalks and aromatics in the broth are there for flavor. Pick out the shrimp and pieces you want to eat.
faq: Is it a restaurant that was added to the UNESCO list?
No. What was inscribed is the knowledge of making tom yum goong and the food culture around it. It does not mean any particular restaurant has been certified.
Is every tom yum a shrimp soup?
No. Goong means shrimp, and there are tom yum soups made with other ingredients. Look at the name that follows tom yum on the menu to help you choose the main ingredient.

green-curry.name: Green Curry
green-curry.scope: Central Thai food culture · eaten across the country
green-curry.intro: If you want a fragrant curry with rice, pick green curry. Green curry paste is stirred into coconut milk, then meat and vegetables are simmered in it. The richness of coconut gets a lift from herbs like basil. The pale green color can look mild, but it has heat, so if you do not handle spicy food well, say so when you order.
green-curry.flavor: Behind the rich, smooth coconut milk, you taste the heat of the curry paste. The herb notes come through clearly, so it tastes quite different from sweeter, milder curries. Spoon a little curry and its pieces over your rice at a time.
green-curry.ingredients: Made with green curry paste and coconut milk, simmered with meat and vegetables. Herbs such as basil sometimes add aroma.
green-curry.story: Green curry is one of the signature dishes of Central Thailand. In Thailand it is eaten not only with steamed rice but also with noodles such as khanom chin, or with roti. On a trip to Bangkok, order a curry with the meat you like and eat it with rice.
green-curry.tip: Even with coconut milk in it, it is still spicy. Ask about the heat when you order.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as chicken, and order. If curry and rice are sold separately on the menu, order the rice too.
Ask whether the heat can be reduced before the dish is made. Coconut milk does not mean the dish is not spicy.
Spoon a little curry sauce and its pieces over your rice at a time. If you are sharing several dishes, you do not have to pour all the curry over the rice at once.
faq: Isn't green curry mild?
It has heat. Coconut milk can make it feel gentle, but the curry paste is made with chilies. If you do not handle spicy food well, ask about the heat before you order.
Is a curry with only vegetables vegetarian?
Not necessarily. The curry paste or seasoning can contain animal-based ingredients. If you are vegetarian, ask not only about the meat but also whether you can eat the paste and sauce.
green-curry.photoAlt: Green curry in a bowl with roti on the side
green-curry.photoCaption: Green curry served with roti · example dish

massaman.name: Massaman Curry
massaman.intro: Try massaman curry, scented with cinnamon and cardamom. It is a rich curry flavored with several spices, a dish to eat slowly with rice. It also suits anyone who wants a different aroma from green curry. It is known as a comparatively mild curry, but the heat level differs from restaurant to restaurant.
massaman.flavor: The aroma of spices such as cinnamon, cardamom and clove runs through the curry. Eating it side by side with green curry, where the herbs stand out, makes the difference between the two easy to taste. Eat the thick sauce with rice a little at a time.
massaman.ingredients: Flavored with several spices, including cinnamon, cardamom and clove. The actual ingredients, such as meat and nuts, depend on the menu item you order.
massaman.story: Massaman is one of Thailand's signature curries and is introduced in guides to Central Thai food culture. It is not a dish eaten only in one city. If Thai curry is new to you, start with massaman, and when you get curious about the flavor of herbs and chilies, try green curry too.
massaman.tip: A comparatively mild curry does not mean it has no heat.
steps: Pick a menu item with the meat you want. It also helps to check whether rice comes with the curry.
Taste a little curry first, then eat it with rice. Spoon some of the thick sauce and meat over the rice together.
If you cannot eat nuts or a particular spice, tell the staff before you order. Even a comparatively mild curry can have some heat.
faq: I'm new to Thai curry. Is massaman a good choice?
It is worth a try if you want to start with a comparatively mild curry. The heat and the spice flavors vary by restaurant, so it helps to ask about the heat when you order.
Is all massaman halal?
You cannot tell from the name of a dish whether it is halal. Check the meat and seasonings used, and the restaurant's certification.
emphasis: does not mean it has no heat

mango-sticky-rice.name: Mango Sticky Rice
mango-sticky-rice.intro: If you want something sweet after a meal, have mango sticky rice. It is a Thai dessert that serves sticky rice flavored with coconut milk beside ripe mango. A bite of mango and sticky rice together brings the fruit's sweetness and the chewy texture into balance. If you have finished a big meal, share a plate with your companions.
mango-sticky-rice.flavor: The sweetness of mango meets the richness of coconut. Sticky rice is chewy, so the texture is different from eating the fruit alone. Taste the mango and the rice separately, then try them together in one spoonful.
mango-sticky-rice.ingredients: Ripe mango served with sticky rice flavored with coconut milk. The sauce and toppings vary from one seller to the next.
mango-sticky-rice.story: In Thailand, sticky rice flavored with coconut milk is eaten as a dessert with a range of toppings. Mango sticky rice is the version served with ripe mango. It includes rice, but think of it as a sweet dessert rather than a meal eaten with side dishes.
mango-sticky-rice.tip: It includes rice, but it is a dish enjoyed as a sweet dessert.
steps: If you are ordering after a meal, look at the size of the plate and decide whether to share.
Take a bite of mango and a bite of sticky rice, then try them together. You can taste how the flavor and texture change when the two meet.
If the sauce comes on the side, add it a little at a time. You do not have to pour it all on at the start.
faq: It has rice in it. Is it a meal?
It is usually enjoyed as a sweet dessert. You eat mango together with sticky rice flavored with coconut milk. If you eat it after a meal, it is fine to share with your companions.
Does the mango always taste the same?
No. It depends on the variety, how ripe it is and when it is sold. It is a dish where sticky rice and coconut sauce are added to the flavor of the mango, so try them together bite by bite.

khao-soi.name: Khao Soi
khao-soi.scope: A signature dish of the North
khao-soi.intro: If you are choosing a meal in Chiang Mai, try khao soi. Egg noodles sit in a coconut curry broth, topped with crispy fried noodles, in this signature dish of the North. Part of the fun is eating soft noodles and crispy noodles by turns. If a lime wedge comes on the side, taste the broth first and then squeeze in a little.
khao-soi.flavor: A rich curry broth and two kinds of noodle texture define it. The noodles on top start out crispy and slowly soften as they touch the broth. Taste the broth before and after you add the condiments and you can enjoy different flavors in a single bowl.
khao-soi.ingredients: Egg noodles in coconut curry broth, topped with fried noodles. Some menus let you choose the main ingredient, such as chicken or beef.
khao-soi.story: Khao soi is a well-known dish on a trip to Chiang Mai, but it is also eaten in other cities of the North. Unlike a Northern meal of sticky rice and side dishes, it puts noodles and broth in one bowl. It is a good pick when you are eating alone or want a simple lunch.
khao-soi.tip: Try the crispy noodles on top first, before they get soaked in the broth.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as chicken or beef, and order.
Take a bite of the fried noodles before the broth soaks them. Eating them alternately with the soft noodles underneath lets you taste the difference in texture.
Taste the broth first, then add the lime and condiments a little at a time. You do not have to put everything in at the start.
faq: Can I only eat it in Chiang Mai?
No. It is a signature dish eaten in many cities of the North. If Chiang Mai is your first taste of Northern food, a bowl of khao soi is a good place to start.
What kind of meat goes in khao soi?
There are several menu items, such as chicken or beef. Look at the main ingredient listed on the menu and choose the one you want. Not every restaurant uses the same meat.
khao-soi.photoAlt: Khao soi topped with fried noodles, with condiments served separately

sai-ua.name: Sai Ua
sai-ua.scope: A signature dish of the North
sai-ua.intro: If you want a fragrant meat dish in Chiang Mai, pick sai ua. It is a Northern sausage made by mixing chilies and herbs into pork and grilling it. One bite gives you the savory taste of grilled meat and the aroma of herbs together. With sticky rice and vegetables, it makes a satisfying Northern Thai meal.
sai-ua.flavor: The savory flavor of pork is joined by herbs and chili seasoning. Its distinctive aroma is different from the sausages you are used to. The heat depends on the recipe, so if you are trying it for the first time, start with a small piece.
sai-ua.ingredients: Pork mixed with chilies, garlic and several herbs, then grilled. The blend of herbs and seasoning differs from place to place.
sai-ua.story: Sai ua often appears on the table of the Lanna North. It is also eaten with sticky rice or with dipping sauces such as nam prik. Order it with nam prik ong, which is seasoned with tomato, and vegetables, and you can alternate between the grilled meat and the sauce.
sai-ua.tip: It is a sausage of pork mixed with herbs and grilled.
steps: Choose how much to eat and order. If you are eating several dishes, it is fine to split a little with your companions.
Start with a small piece. Once you know the herb aroma and the heat, it is easier to decide how much sticky rice and vegetables to eat with it.
Eat it with sticky rice, nam prik and vegetables. You get a different meal from eating the sausage alone.
faq: Is it the same sausage as sai krok Isan?
No. Sai ua is a grilled Northern sausage with herbs. Sai krok Isan is an Isan dish made by fermenting pork and rice, and its tangy flavor from fermentation is its trait.
Can I order it if I do not eat pork?
The typical sai ua is made with pork. If you do not eat pork, it is better to choose another dish for your meal.

nam-prik-ong.name: Nam Prik Ong
nam-prik-ong.scope: A dipping sauce of the North
nam-prik-ong.intro: Meet nam prik ong, a sauce eaten with vegetables at Northern Thai meals. It is a red dipping sauce made from tomatoes, ground pork and chilies. Dab a little on vegetables or eat it with sticky rice, and you taste the savory depth of pork and the tang of tomato together. Order it with sai ua to set a Northern Thai table.
nam-prik-ong.flavor: Chili seasoning is added to the tangy tomato and the savory pork. The smooth sauce goes with crunchy vegetables and the two textures work together. The heat differs from place to place.
nam-prik-ong.ingredients: Made with tomatoes, ground pork and chilies. It is a sauce you eat a little at a time with sticky rice and vegetables.
nam-prik-ong.story: Nam prik is a dipping sauce eaten with vegetables or rice in Thailand. The North has many kinds of nam prik, and nam prik ong is the type made with tomatoes and pork. You can find it with sticky rice and vegetables at a khantoke meal, where food is set out on small tables.
nam-prik-ong.tip: Even a tomato sauce has ground pork in it.
steps: Check that sticky rice and vegetables come with it, and order it with other Northern dishes.
Dab a little sauce on a vegetable and try it first. Eaten with sticky rice, it gives you a different texture.
It is a pork dish even though it is a tomato sauce. If you avoid meat or animal-based seasonings, tell the staff before you order.
faq: Is it vegetarian if it is made with tomatoes?
No. The typical nam prik ong contains ground pork. If you are vegetarian, do not choose it by the tomato color alone. Ask about the meat and the seasonings too.
Do you eat the sauce on its own?
You eat it a little at a time with vegetables, sticky rice and so on. Order it with grilled dishes such as sai ua and you can share a range of flavors.
nam-prik-ong.photoAlt: Nam prik ong, a tomato and pork sauce, with vegetables

mi-hokkien.name: Mi Hokkien
mi-hokkien.scope: A local noodle dish of Phuket
mi-hokkien.intro: If you want noodles in Phuket, try mi hokkien. Thick yellow noodles are stir-fried over high heat with seafood and sauce. You enjoy the sauce soaked into the noodles and the seafood together. It is a good pick for lunch on a day exploring Old Phuket Town.
mi-hokkien.flavor: The thick noodles carry the flavor of the sauce and seafood. Compared with mi hun, which uses thin rice noodles, the texture of the noodles feels different. The taste of a bowl can change with the amount of broth and with extras such as egg.
mi-hokkien.ingredients: Thick yellow noodles stir-fried with seafood and sauce. Meat or egg is sometimes used, so look at what else goes in on the menu.
mi-hokkien.story: The food of Phuket carries the food culture that Chinese residents have kept going. Mi hokkien is a signature noodle dish shaped by that influence. If you have only thought of grilled seafood in Phuket, try this dish, where seafood and noodles are stir-fried together, for a different meal.
mi-hokkien.tip: It is a different noodle dish from mi hun, which uses thin rice noodles.
steps: Look at which ingredients go in, such as seafood, meat or egg, and choose the menu item you want.
When the dish arrives, eat the noodles and seafood together. You can taste the sauce soaked into the thick noodles.
If there is extra seasoning, taste first and add it a little at a time. If you cannot eat seafood, ask whether it is also in the broth and sauce.
faq: Is it the same noodle dish as mi hun?

No. Mi hokkien is a signature Phuket noodle dish made with thick yellow noodles, while mi hun uses thin rice noodles. If you try both, you notice that the noodle texture and what is served with them are different.
Can I order it if I cannot eat seafood?
The typical mi hokkien has seafood in it. Whether the ingredients can be swapped depends on the restaurant, so ask not only about the main ingredient but also about the broth and sauce.
emphasis: different noodle dish from mi hun

mi-hun.name: Mi Hun
mi-hun.scope: A local noodle dish of Phuket
mi-hun.intro: In Phuket, try mi hun too, made with thin rice noodles. It is known as a dish served with a pork rib broth. Take a bite of noodles and then a spoonful of the warm broth, and it tastes different from eating the noodles alone. It is a good choice when you have had thick-noodle mi hokkien and wonder about another noodle dish.
mi-hun.flavor: You enjoy the texture of thin rice noodles together with the flavor of the broth served with them. If the noodles and broth come separately, alternate between them. It makes for a different meal from thick stir-fried noodles.
mi-hun.ingredients: Made with thin rice noodles. The form served with a pork rib broth is the best known.
mi-hun.story: In Phuket you can find thin rice noodle dishes under names such as mi hun and mi hun bar chang. Serving them with a pork rib broth is the best-known form. How each restaurant serves it can differ, so check the menu to see whether the noodles and broth come together.
mi-hun.tip: Check whether the pork rib broth comes with it before you order.
steps: Check the menu to see whether the pork rib broth comes with it, then order.
Take a bite of noodles first, then sip the warm broth. Alternate between the noodles and the broth.
If you cannot eat pork, ask about what goes into the noodle seasoning and the broth. Do not assume that leaving out the broth is enough to avoid pork.
faq: Do the noodles and broth always come together?
It depends on the restaurant and the menu item. The form served with a pork rib broth is well known, but look at what the item you order includes before you choose.
If I do not eat pork, can I just skip the broth?
Pork can also be used in the noodle seasoning and the cooking. If you avoid pork, ask about the ingredients of both the noodles and the broth.

o-aew.name: O-Aew
o-aew.intro: If you want a break on a hot day while walking around Old Phuket Town, try o-aew. It is a cold treat with jelly, sweet syrup and toppings over ice. Scoop up the ice and jelly together and you enjoy the coolness and the soft texture at once. It also works as dessert after you finish a noodle meal.
o-aew.flavor: Sweet syrup and soft jelly join the cold ice. The taste and texture of each spoonful changes with the toppings you add. Scoop up ice and jelly together.
o-aew.ingredients: Ice and jelly with sweet syrup and toppings. The ingredients of the jelly and toppings differ from shop to shop.
o-aew.story: O-aew is a local dessert of Phuket. The table in Phuket includes cold treats like this as well as seafood and noodle dishes. It is worth trying when you want something sweet between meals on a trip.
o-aew.tip: Scooping ice and jelly together lets you enjoy both textures.
steps: Look at which jelly and toppings go on it and choose. You can also ask whether the syrup can be adjusted.
Scoop up a spoonful of ice and jelly together. The texture is different from eating the jelly alone.
If there is an ingredient you avoid, ask what the jelly and toppings are made from. Even when sold under the same name, the makeup is not always the same.
faq: Is o-aew a meal?
It is a snack made with ice and jelly. Have it as a break on a hot day or as dessert after a meal.
Are the jelly and toppings the same everywhere?
No. The toppings and syrup can differ from shop to shop. If there is an ingredient you cannot eat, ask about the jelly and toppings together.

boat-noodles.name: Boat Noodles
boat-noodles.intro: If you want a bowl of noodles while touring the ruins in Ayutthaya, try boat noodles. Noodles and meat are served in broth, and along with grilled river prawns it is one of the best-known dishes in Ayutthaya. Choose the noodles and meat on the menu, then enjoy it with the broth while it is hot. They are eaten in other cities too, but it is a good meal to pick on a trip to Ayutthaya.
boat-noodles.flavor: You enjoy the broth, noodles and meat together. The taste of the broth can change with the meat and the seasonings. Try it first without adding any seasoning, then add chili or other seasonings a little at a time.
boat-noodles.ingredients: Noodles and meat served in broth. How meat, offal and seasonings are used differs by menu item.
boat-noodles.story: On a food trip in Ayutthaya, you can try boat noodles, grilled river prawns and roti sai mai together. A day that has noodles for lunch and roti sai mai as a snack sounds good. Still, boat noodles are not something you can only eat in Ayutthaya.
boat-noodles.tip: Order after looking at the noodle type, the meat and the bowl size.
steps: Choose the noodles and meat you want and order. If you avoid meat, offal or a particular seasoning, also ask what goes into the broth.
Look at the bowl size and decide how many bowls you will eat. Not every shop serves the same size.
Taste the broth first, then add extra seasoning a little at a time. You do not have to add a lot of chili at the start.
faq: Can I only eat it in Ayutthaya?
No. It is a dish eaten in other cities too. In Ayutthaya, it makes a good meal to pick between sights at the ruins.
Are the ingredients in the broth always the same?
No. The meat, offal, seasonings and broth differ by menu item. If there is something you avoid, ask whether it is used in the broth too, instead of just asking to leave out the meat.

river-prawns.name: Grilled River Prawns
river-prawns.intro: If you are looking for a meal to share in Ayutthaya, pick grilled river prawns. The prawns are grilled and you peel the meat to eat it, so it suits a group with rice and other dishes. The price changes with the size of the prawns and the selling unit, so look at the prawns you will order first and then choose.
river-prawns.flavor: You enjoy the aroma of grilled prawns and the texture of the meat. Try the meat on its own first, then add a little of the sauce that comes with it. Eat it with rice and you taste the sauce too.
river-prawns.ingredients: River prawns, grilled. The size of the prawns, the sauce served with them and the selling unit differ from restaurant to restaurant.
river-prawns.story: River prawns are a well-known ingredient on a trip to Ayutthaya. If boat noodles are a one-bowl meal, grilled river prawns are a dish to pick when you share with your companions. You do not have to assume from the name river prawns that they are wild or that they were caught in the rivers of Ayutthaya.
river-prawns.tip: Ask whether the unit is per prawn or by weight.
steps: Ask first whether the price is per prawn or by weight. Even for the same grilled prawns, the price differs with size and the way they are sold.
Decide the size and the number of prawns and get the order total. It also helps to check whether rice and other dishes are included.
Peel the prawn and eat it as it is first. Add a little sauce and share with your companions.
faq: Are they all prawns caught in the rivers of Ayutthaya?
You cannot tell from the name of the dish alone. If you want to know the real origin and whether they are farmed, ask about the prawns you are going to order.
How much should I expect to pay?

It depends on the size of the prawns and how they are sold, such as per prawn or by weight. If you get the price for the size and number you chose before you order, it is easier to set the cost of the meal.
river-prawns.photoAlt: Split grilled river prawns with sauce

roti-sai-mai.name: Roti Sai Mai
roti-sai-mai.intro: In Ayutthaya, try roti sai mai, a thin roti wrapped around spun sugar. You lay fine strands of sugar on the roti and roll it up to eat. When you wrap it yourself, add the spun sugar a little at a time and you can set the sweetness you want. With your companions, unfold the roti one sheet at a time and share.
roti-sai-mai.flavor: The thin, soft roti and the fine strands of spun sugar work together in texture. The sweetness depends on how much spun sugar you add. Put in only a little at first, and add more to suit your taste on the next roti.
roti-sai-mai.ingredients: Thin roti wrapped around fine strands of spun sugar. There are forms where the roti is scented with pandan or has sesame added.
roti-sai-mai.story: Roti sai mai is linked to the snack culture that the Muslim community of Ayutthaya has kept going. Some roti is green from pandan scent, and some uses sesame. What sets this snack apart from a regular roti menu is that you wrap spun sugar in it.
roti-sai-mai.tip: Add the spun sugar a little at a time and you can eat it as sweet as you like.
steps: Get the roti and the spun sugar together. If they come separately, open out one sheet of roti.
Lay a little spun sugar on it, then roll or fold the roti and eat it.
If you want more sweetness, add a little more spun sugar to the next roti. You do not have to add a lot at once.
faq: How is it different from regular roti?
It is a thin roti wrapped around fine strands of spun sugar. The way you eat it and the texture are different from roti made with banana or other toppings.
Is green roti the same snack?
There is a form in which pandan-scented roti is wrapped around spun sugar. The actual scent and ingredients can differ from seller to seller.
roti-sai-mai.photoAlt: Spun sugar laid on thin roti

som-tam.name: Som Tam (Papaya Salad)
som-tam.scope: A signature Isan dish · eaten across the country
som-tam.intro: If you want something crunchy and tangy, try som tam. It is a salad made by shredding unripe papaya and pounding it with seasoning in a mortar. Sourness and heat soak into the papaya, and it goes well with sticky rice or grilled dishes. In Isan, some versions include a fermented fish seasoning, so if the fermented aroma is unfamiliar, ask which kind of som tam it is when you order.
som-tam.flavor: Sour and spicy seasoning meets the crunch of papaya. In versions with pla ra, a fermented fish seasoning, you can also taste a fermented aroma. Even with the same som tam, the taste changes with how the seasoning and chilies are used.
som-tam.ingredients: Unripe papaya seasoned with chilies and a sour ingredient. Peanuts, shrimp and fermented fish seasoning depend on the kind of som tam.
som-tam.story: Som tam is a signature Isan dish and is eaten in many cities across Thailand. Even within Isan, each area has a different kind, so you can compare som tam much as you might compare regional barbecue styles. On a trip to Khon Kaen, eat it with sticky rice and other Isan dishes.
som-tam.tip: If you want less heat, say so before it is made.
steps: Choose the kind of som tam and ask whether it uses a fermented fish seasoning such as pla ra.
If you want less heat, say so before it is made. Once the papaya has been pounded with the seasoning, it is hard to take out just the chilies.
Order sticky rice and other dishes with it and eat a little at a time. You get a different meal from eating papaya alone.
faq: Does som tam taste the same wherever you eat it?
No. The chilies, the seasonings and the way sweetness is added differ. If the aroma of fermentation is unfamiliar, it helps to ask first whether pla ra goes in.
It is a papaya salad, so is it vegetarian?
Not necessarily. Some kinds use fish seasoning or shrimp. If you are vegetarian, ask whether you can eat the seasoning and toppings as well as the papaya.

larb.name: Larb
larb.intro: If you want a meat dish to eat with sticky rice, try Isan-style larb. Minced meat is seasoned with herbs, lime and toasted rice powder. The tang and the nutty aroma join the flavor of the meat, and it goes well with vegetables. Some versions use raw meat, so when you order, ask whether the larb is made with cooked meat.
larb.flavor: The tang of lime and the aroma of herbs are joined by the nutty flavor of toasted rice powder. The seasoning is evenly mixed into the minced meat, so it is good to eat a little at a time with sticky rice. The taste also changes with the meat used, such as pork, beef or duck.
larb.ingredients: Minced meat seasoned with toasted rice powder, herbs, lime and more. The meat varies, including pork, beef and duck.
larb.story: Larb is a meat salad you find on the Isan table. The North has larb too, but the seasoning and the cooking are not the same. The dish introduced here is Isan-style larb, with toasted rice powder, lime and herbs added.
larb.tip: Some kinds use raw meat. Order cooked larb.
steps: Choose the meat you want, then order it as a cooked dish. There is larb made with raw meat as well.
If you want less heat, tell the staff before the dish is made.
Eat it with sticky rice and vegetables. Eat the larb a little at a time and enjoy the flavor of the meat and herbs.
faq: Is larb always made with cooked meat?
No. Some kinds use raw meat. The Tourism Authority of Thailand advises ordering cooked larb, so say so when you order.
Does Northern larb taste the same?

The seasoning and cooking are different. This guide covers Isan-style larb, which uses toasted rice powder, lime and herbs. Even when you see the same name in the North, it can feel like a different dish.
larb.photoCaption: Isan-style larb made with duck · example dish

sai-krok-isan.name: Sai Krok Isan
sai-krok-isan.intro: If you want to taste the tangy fermented foods of Isan, try sai krok Isan. It is a sausage made by fermenting pork with rice, garlic and more. The savory taste of meat is joined by the sourness that comes from fermentation. If you have tried sai ua, the Northern sausage, compare the two.
sai-krok-isan.flavor: Its traits are the savory pork and the tang that comes from fermentation. The strength of the sourness depends on the degree of fermentation and the cooking. The raw chilies served with it can be hot, so eat them separately, a little at a time.
sai-krok-isan.ingredients: Pork mixed with rice, garlic and more, then fermented. The sourness can change with the fermentation and the way it is cooked.
sai-krok-isan.story: Sai krok Isan is an Isan dish made by fermenting pork and rice. It is not a dish eaten only in Khon Kaen. Comparing it with sai ua, the Northern sausage that celebrates herbal aroma, shows how the ingredients and flavor of sausages differ by region.
sai-krok-isan.tip: Eat the raw chilies served with it separately, a little at a time.
steps: Order carefully, telling apart sai ua, which has herbs, from sai krok Isan, the fermented sausage.
Try the cooked sausage a little at a time. Tasting first shows you how tangy the fermentation is.
If raw chilies come with it, add them separately a little at a time instead of eating them all at once.
faq: Why does a sausage taste sour?
Because it is made by fermenting pork and rice. It is a sausage enjoyed for the tang from fermentation, and how sour it actually is depends on the product and the cooking.
How is it different from sai ua?
Sai ua is a grilled Northern sausage with herbs, while sai krok Isan is an Isan sausage of fermented pork and rice. If you try both, you can compare the herbal aroma and the sourness of fermentation.

au-pla.name: Au Pla
au-pla.scope: A local dish of Khon Kaen
au-pla.intro: If you want to try a local dish in Khon Kaen that is different from som tam, look for au pla. It is a curry made with freshwater fish, spicy and salty. If you like fish, it is worth choosing as a dish to eat with rice. The fish and seasonings used can differ from restaurant to restaurant.
au-pla.flavor: It is a curry that adds heat and saltiness to freshwater fish. You get a different meal from foods like som tam, where you eat crunchy vegetables, or meat dishes such as larb. Eat a little at a time with rice.
au-pla.ingredients: A curry made with freshwater fish. The fish and seasonings used depend on the menu item you order.
au-pla.story: Isan has a culture of using river fish in its food. Au pla is introduced as a local dish of Khon Kaen among them. It suits someone who has had som tam and larb, known across Isan, and wants to learn about other food in Khon Kaen.
au-pla.tip: Eat slowly and watch for fish bones.
steps: Find au pla on the menu and ask what fish is used. It also helps to ask whether the heat can be adjusted.
Order rice to eat with it and have the fish and broth a little at a time.
Eat slowly and watch for fish bones. The kind of fish and the detailed seasoning depend on the menu item you order.
faq: How is it different from som tam or larb?
Au pla is a curry made with freshwater fish. Unlike som tam, where papaya is pounded, or larb, where minced meat is seasoned, you can eat the fish and broth with rice.
Is it a dish connected to Khon Kaen?
Yes. It is a dish the Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces as a local dish of Khon Kaen. If you want to taste a freshwater fish dish on an Isan trip, it is worth a look.

hat-yai-chicken.name: Hat Yai Fried Chicken
hat-yai-chicken.scope: The signature dish of Hat Yai
hat-yai-chicken.intro: In Hat Yai, try crispy fried chicken served with fried shallots. It is Hat Yai fried chicken, a dish known by the name of the city. The crispy chicken gets the savory aroma of shallots, and it goes well with sticky rice. Put a little of the shallots that come with it on top of the chicken and take a bite.
hat-yai-chicken.flavor: You enjoy the crispness of the fried chicken and the savory flavor of the shallots together. It is also characterized by seasoning with aromatics such as garlic, coriander root and white pepper. You can eat just the chicken and shallots before you add any sauce.
hat-yai-chicken.ingredients: Fried chicken served with fried shallots. Garlic, coriander root and white pepper go into the seasoning, and it is known as a dish eaten with sticky rice.
hat-yai-chicken.story: Hat Yai is a city of the Songkhla area, where the food culture of Chinese and Muslim communities sits side by side. Hat Yai fried chicken is known as a signature dish of this area. It is sold in other cities too, but if you are in Hat Yai, have it as a meal with sticky rice.
hat-yai-chicken.tip: Eat the fried shallots together with the chicken for more savory flavor.
steps: Choose the pieces and the number you want. If you are with a group, it is fine to order the pieces each person wants.
See whether sticky rice and sauce come with it and order more of what you need.
First eat the chicken and the fried shallots together. Next, add a little sauce for a different taste.
faq: Can I only eat it in Hat Yai?
No. Other areas sell Hat Yai-style fried chicken as well. If you are in Hat Yai, it is a good idea to try the dish known by the name of the city with sticky rice.
Is every chicken dish halal?
No. You cannot tell from the type of meat whether a dish is halal. If you need a halal meal, check the restaurant's certification and the actual ingredients and cooking conditions.
hat-yai-chicken.photoAlt: Hat Yai-style fried chicken with plenty of fried shallots
hat-yai-chicken.photoCaption: Hat Yai-style fried chicken · example dish

bak-kut-teh.name: Bak Kut Teh
bak-kut-teh.scope: A Chinese-style dish enjoyed in the Songkhla area
bak-kut-teh.intro: If you want a meal with warm broth on a trip to Hat Yai, pick bak kut teh. Pork ribs are simmered with herbs and aromatic spices. In the Songkhla area it is introduced as a broth dish with the aroma of Chinese herbs. If you eat pork, enjoy it slowly with rice.
bak-kut-teh.flavor: The aroma of herbs and spices joins the broth of simmered pork ribs. The color and richness of the broth differ with the recipe. Alternate between the ribs and the broth and enjoy the fragrance.
bak-kut-teh.ingredients: Pork ribs simmered with herbs and aromatic spices. Extras and sides differ from menu to menu.
bak-kut-teh.story: Bak kut teh is one of the Chinese-style dishes you find in the Songkhla area. It does not mean it was first made in Hat Yai. On a day when you want a different meal from crispy fried chicken, have a meal of pork rib broth and rice.
bak-kut-teh.tip: The broth uses pork too. If you avoid pork, choose another dish.
steps: First think about whether this is a menu item for you and the companions who eat pork. The typical bak kut teh uses pork ribs.
Check whether rice and sides come with it, then order.
Eat the ribs and sip the broth a little at a time. Enjoy the aroma of the herbs and spices with rice.
faq: Is bak kut teh a dish that began in Hat Yai?
It is not presented as a dish that originated in Hat Yai. It is a Chinese-style dish you find in the Songkhla area, and a menu item that lets you see the varied food culture of the area.
Can someone who does not eat pork have it?
The typical bak kut teh contains pork ribs. If you avoid pork, it is better to choose another dish. Keep in mind that even eating only the broth means eating a dish made with pork.

roti.name: Roti
roti.intro: If you want a sweet snack on the street, try roti. A thinly stretched dough is cooked on a griddle and served with sweet sauces such as condensed milk or chocolate. There are versions with banana, so it is a good pick when you want fruit and a snack together. If the vendor cuts the roti for you, share it a piece at a time while it is warm.
roti.flavor: You enjoy the thin griddled dough and the sweet sauce together. The crispness at the edges and the softness inside change with the ingredients and how it is cooked. In a version with banana, you taste the fruit's sweetness too.
roti.ingredients: A griddled dough served with sauces such as condensed milk and chocolate. Whether it has banana or egg depends on the menu item.
roti.story: In Thailand, roti is also found as a sweet street snack. Roti sai mai from Ayutthaya is a thin roti wrapped around spun sugar, and it is eaten differently from the griddled roti introduced here. If you try both, you get different snacks under the same name of roti.
roti.tip: Banana and sauce differ by menu item. Pick the toppings you want first.
steps: Choose plain roti or roti with banana or another filling, and tell the vendor which sauce you want.
If you want less condensed milk or sauce, ask before it is cooked. It is hard to reduce the amount once the sauce has been drizzled on.
Share the cut roti a piece at a time while it is warm.
faq: Is it the same snack as roti sai mai?
No. Roti sai mai is an Ayutthaya snack of thin roti wrapped around spun sugar. This guide covers street roti, griddled dough served with a sweet sauce.
Can I order it if I cannot eat egg or milk?
Ask about what goes into the dough, the toppings and the sauce, all together. Even a menu item without egg can have an ingredient you avoid in the dough or the condensed milk.
emphasis: Pick the toppings you want first
roti.photoCaption: Thai roti photographed at the Bang Luang Mosque. Toppings and shape differ from shop to shop.

watermelon-shake.name: Watermelon Shake (Taeng Mo Pan)
watermelon-shake.intro: If you want something cold while walking around Thailand on a hot day, try taeng mo pan. It is a watermelon shake made by blending watermelon with water and ice. Unlike watermelon juice you drink like plain water, the ice is blended in so it is enjoyed ice cold. If you want less sweetness, ask for less syrup or sugar when you order.
watermelon-shake.flavor: The flavor of watermelon is joined by the cold, slushy texture of finely blended ice. The taste of a cup changes with the ratio of watermelon to ice and with any added sweetener.
watermelon-shake.ingredients: Watermelon blended with water and ice. Added ingredients such as sugar and syrup differ from shop to shop.
watermelon-shake.story: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces taeng mo pan as a signature fruit drink made by blending watermelon with water and ice. On a trip to Thailand, you can enjoy familiar watermelon as a street drink. Watermelon is a fruit sold year-round, but whether a shop actually sells the drink differs from shop to shop.
watermelon-shake.tip: If you want less added sugar or syrup, say so before it is made.
steps: Choose the taeng mo pan or watermelon shake menu item and check the cup size and the price.
Ask before the drink is made whether the sweetness can be reduced. Even without syrup, the watermelon itself is sweet.
When the blended drink with ice arrives, enjoy it while it is cold.
faq: Is taeng mo pan watermelon juice?
It is a shake made by blending watermelon with water and ice. Because ice is blended in, the texture is different from a drink of pressed watermelon juice only.
If I skip the sugar, does it lose its sweetness?
The watermelon's own sweetness stays. The sugar or syrup that adds sweetness depends on the shop, so ask for less or none before the drink is made.

mango.name: Mango
mango.intro: If you want something sweet in Thailand, try a ripe mango. Varieties such as nam dok mai are known for soft, fragrant yellow flesh. If you have had mango sticky rice, try the fruit on its own to taste the mango itself. Some kinds of unripe mango are eaten crisp and tart.
mango.taste: Ripe mango is soft and sweet. Some varieties of green mango are eaten for a different texture from ripe ones, so you do not need to assume that every green mango is unripe.
mango.why: Thailand has many mango varieties, including nam dok mai and maha chanok, and a food culture that enjoys ripe and green fruit in different ways. It is also familiar as a dessert served over sticky rice, which makes it a good fruit to try on a trip to Thailand.
mango.buying: If you want sweet, soft mango, say you are looking for ripe mango. Crisp mango may be sold separately. The price unit differs between whole fruit bought by the kilogram and a pack of cut fruit.
steps: Wash whole mangoes, then cut the flesh from both sides of the pit.
Cut the flesh into bite-size pieces and eat it as it is or with mango sticky rice.
If you want to buy some to eat now and some to take along, pick the ripeness together with the seller.
mango.regional: Nam dok mai Si Thong of Phitsanulok: harvest listed for Mar–Jun
mango.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a mango looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

durian.name: Durian
durian.intro: If its strong smell has made you hesitate, try just a little durian. Inside the spiky husk is rich yellow flesh. It is a fruit where you taste the aroma and the soft, sweet flesh together. If it is your first time, start with a small portion of flesh from a seller rather than buying a whole fruit.
durian.taste: Its traits are a sweet, rich taste and creamy flesh. How firm the flesh is and how strong the smell is vary with the variety, such as monthong and chanee, and with ripeness.
durian.why: Thai durian varieties such as monthong, chanee and kan yao are well known. It is also a fruit people feel strongly about because of its strong smell and sweet, rich flesh. You can eat it as it is or enjoy it as ice cream and desserts.
durian.buying: Ask first whether the price tag is per kilogram of whole fruit with the husk or per kilogram of prepared flesh. If you want to take it to a hotel or onto transportation, check the rules on bringing it in first.
steps: If it is your first time, buy a small amount of flesh and taste it.
If you choose a whole fruit, ask about the variety, ripeness and the price including the husk, and have it opened for you.
Take out the large seeds and eat the flesh. Before you carry durian to your lodging, check whether it is allowed.
durian.regional: Sisaket volcanic-soil durian: harvest listed for May–Jun
durian.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a durian looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

mangosteen.name: Mangosteen
mangosteen.intro: Try a mangosteen, where a purple rind opens to segments of white flesh. You get sweetness and tartness together, and it is juicy. The name has mango in it, but it is a different fruit from mango. It is also good to share a few after a meal with your companions.
mangosteen.taste: The white flesh is soft and sweet-tart. A large segment may contain a seed, so eat slowly.
mangosteen.why: The appeal lies in the purple rind, the white flesh and a sweet but fresh taste. In Thailand it is harvested in different regions at different times, so look for it according to the season you travel.
mangosteen.buying: Check the rind for damage and pick fruit to eat right away. Because the rind is thick on whole fruit, the per-kilogram price is not the weight of the flesh you eat alone.
steps: Press the rind open, or cut only shallowly around it and open it up.
Take out the white flesh and check for a seed inside the larger segments.
Be careful that the red juice from the rind does not get on your clothes.
mangosteen.regional: Southern Khao Khiriwong mangosteen: harvest listed for Jul–Dec
mangosteen.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a mangosteen looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

rambutan.name: Rambutan
rambutan.availability: Harvest period varies by growing region
rambutan.intro: Meet the rambutan, a red fruit with hair-like spines on its rind. Peel it and you find white flesh with sweet juice. The outside looks unfamiliar, but removing the rind and seed is simple. It is worth buying just a few at a market to try.
rambutan.taste: The white flesh is sweet and juicy. Some varieties, such as the Thai rong rian, differ in texture and in how easily the flesh comes off the seed.
rambutan.why: The hairy-looking rind stands out, with white flesh inside. The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces Rong Rian rambutan of Na San, Surat Thani, as a regional GI fruit.
rambutan.buying: Ask whether it is sold by the kilogram or in a fixed bag. Pick only what you will eat right away, peel it and remove the seed.
steps: Make a shallow slit in the rind, then open it and peel it off.
Eat the white flesh and take out the seed in the middle.
If it is sold in a bag, look at the weight and the price together before you buy.
rambutan.regional: Na San Rong Rian rambutan: harvest listed for Jul–Aug

longan.name: Longan
longan.intro: If you are curious about the fruit of Chiang Mai and the North, try longan. It is a small fruit with a thin brown rind, translucent flesh and a black seed inside. Peel and eat them one at a time to enjoy the sweetness. Dried longan and fresh fruit have different textures, so it is good to start with fresh.
longan.taste: The flesh is sweet, and the aroma differs with the variety. There is a black seed inside the white flesh, so remove it as you eat.
longan.why: It is a good fruit to learn about together with Northern Thailand. Biao Kiao longan of Lamphun is introduced as a regional GI fruit, and it is a fruit enjoyed dried as well as fresh.
longan.buying: Look at whether it is sold in bunches with the stems or as loose fruit. Compare it easily by choosing from the variety and weight on the price tag.
steps: Make a slit in the rind and peel it off by hand.
Remove the black seed when you eat the flesh.
If you also want to buy dried longan, check the price and package weight separately from fresh fruit.
longan.regional: Lamphun Biao Kiao longan: harvest listed for Jul–Sep
longan.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what longan looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

lychee.name: Lychee
lychee.availability: Timing varies by growing region and variety
lychee.intro: If you want fragrant, juicy fruit, try lychee. Peel the red rind and you find white flesh, and one bite gives you sweetness and aroma together. If you have had it in a drink or a dessert, try the fresh fruit in season too.
lychee.taste: The white flesh is sweet, and some varieties have a tart note. Peel the rind and eat the flesh, removing the seed in the middle.
lychee.why: Thai lychee varieties such as Hong Huai and Chakkraphat are well known. Kom lychee of Samut Songkhram is also introduced as a regional GI fruit, so it is a good fruit for comparing growing regions.
lychee.buying: Separate the unit when whole fruit is sold by the kilogram from when it is sold in a fixed pack. The harvest period for fresh fruit may differ from when lychee drinks are on the menu.
steps: Peel off the rind and take out the flesh.
Remove the seed in the middle and eat the flesh.
If you want to buy a package to take home separately from fruit to eat now, tell the seller how much you need.
lychee.regional: Samut Songkhram Kom lychee: harvest listed for Apr–May
lychee.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what lychee looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

longkong.name: Longkong
longkong.availability: Harvest period varies by growing region
longkong.intro: Meet longkong, small brownish fruit that hang in bunches. Peel the thin rind and the translucent flesh comes out in segments. The name is close to longan, but the shape and the way it eats are different. If you see both fruits side by side at a market, buy a little of each and compare.
longkong.taste: You can taste both sweetness and tartness in the translucent flesh. If a segment has a seed, take it out instead of chewing it.
longkong.why: Part of the fun is peeling small fruit one at a time from the bunch. Tanyong Mat longkong of Narathiwat in the South is known as a regional GI fruit, so it is a good fruit to learn about together with its growing region.
longkong.buying: Longan and longkong are different fruits. If you order after looking at both the name and the look of the bunch, it is easy to get the fruit you want.
steps: Pull one fruit off the bunch.
Peel the rind and eat the flesh.
The seed can taste bitter, so remove any seeds you see and eat slowly.
longkong.regional: Tanyong Mat longkong: harvest listed for Aug–Sep

pomelo.name: Pomelo
pomelo.intro: Try a pomelo, which looks like a giant grapefruit. Peel the thick rind and remove the membrane, and the granules of flesh appear. Sweetness and tartness feel different depending on the variety. If using a knife at your lodging is hard, you can choose prepared pomelo sold in a pack.
pomelo.taste: It is a citrus fruit where you feel the granules of flesh. The color and the sweetness and tartness differ by variety, with flesh that is yellowish or pinkish.
pomelo.why: Thailand has several pomelo varieties, such as khao nam phueng and thong dee. Large whole fruit is sometimes prepared and sold as flesh only, which makes it an easy fruit to try while traveling.
pomelo.buying: Tell apart the price per fruit, the price per kilogram and the price of a prepared pack. Whole fruit with its rind and a pack of flesh only are hard to compare directly by the same weight.
steps: Peel off the thick outer rind of whole fruit first.
Separate the segments, remove the inner membrane and take out the flesh.
Remove the seeds and eat the flesh. A prepared pack is easy to share right away.
pomelo.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a pomelo looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.intro: If you want something sweet and tangy on a hot day, try pineapple. You can cut the yellow flesh and eat it piece by piece, or drink it as juice. Thailand has pineapple that differs in crunch and sweetness by variety and growing region. Instead of buying a whole fruit, a prepared bag is an easy way to eat it.
pineapple.taste: You taste sweetness and tartness together, and how firm the flesh is differs by variety. If seasoning is served on the side, taste the fruit first and then add a little.
pineapple.why: It is grown in many parts of Thailand, and there are regional fruits introduced as GI, such as Si Thong pineapple of Trat. It is familiar as whole fruit, prepared fruit and a drink.
pineapple.buying: First look at whether the price is per kilogram of whole fruit, per piece or per bag of cut pieces. The cost of preparing it and the amount you eat differ.
steps: Remove the rind and the tough parts of whole fruit before you eat it.
Cut it into bite-size pieces to share, or pick a prepared bag.
If seasoning comes with it, add a little at a time and eat it the way you like.
pineapple.regional: Trat Si Thong pineapple: harvest listed as year-round
pineapple.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a pineapple looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

banana.name: Banana
banana.availability: Varies by variety and growing region
banana.intro: In Thailand you can find everything from small bananas to bananas of many shapes. Besides eating them fresh, there are menu items where they go into roti or are grilled. If you are looking for a simple snack on the street, take a look at roti with banana too.
banana.taste: The sweetness and the firmness of the flesh vary with the variety and ripeness. It helps to tell apart bananas eaten when yellow and ripe from bananas used for cooking.
banana.why: It is a familiar fruit used in many Thai dishes and snacks. Kluai Khai banana of Kamphaeng Phet is introduced as a regional GI fruit. If you have only pictured one kind of banana, look for varieties of other shapes and sizes at the market.
banana.buying: Bananas are sometimes sold by the bunch rather than by the kilogram. See how many fruits are in a bunch, and if you want to eat them right away, pick ripe ones.
steps: Ask whether the price is for a bunch or for a certain number of fruits.
For bananas to eat right away, pick ripe ones, peel them and eat.
Banana roti and grilled banana are different menu items from whole fruit, so look at their prices separately.
banana.regional: Kamphaeng Phet Kluai Khai banana: harvest listed as year-round
banana.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a banana looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

coconut.name: Young Coconut
coconut.intro: If you want cold coconut water on a hot day, pick a young coconut. The top is opened for you, so you drink the water inside and can scoop out the soft flesh. The fragrant nam hom coconut is a well-known variety in Thailand. When you are thirsty, it is also fine to share one with a companion.
coconut.taste: With a young coconut you enjoy the water and the soft white flesh together. Nam hom is introduced as a variety known for its aroma.
coconut.why: Thailand's fragrant young coconut is a fruit where you drink the water and eat the flesh too. Aromatic coconut of Ban Phaeo, Samut Sakhon, is also introduced as a regional GI fruit.
coconut.buying: Coconuts are sometimes sold one at a time. Coconut water packed in a bottle and a coconut opened for you are not the same product, so look at the menu items separately.
steps: Pick a coconut to drink right away and ask the seller to open the top.
After you drink the coconut water, scoop out the soft flesh with a spoon if you have one.
Order after telling apart the price of one coconut and the price of a bottled drink.
coconut.regional: Ban Phaeo nam hom coconut: harvest listed as year-round
coconut.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a young coconut looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.intro: In Thailand, enjoy watermelon as a drink too. Besides cold sliced watermelon, there is taeng mo pan, blended with ice. It is worth trying on a day when you want something cold while walking. If you only want the fruit, buy cut watermelon and share it with your companions.
watermelon.taste: It is a crunchy, juicy fruit. Fresh fruit and taeng mo pan, blended with ice, give you different textures.
watermelon.why: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces the watermelon shake as a signature fruit drink. Even a familiar fruit can be met in a different way on a trip, as taeng mo pan.
watermelon.buying: Tell apart the price per kilogram of whole watermelon, a bag of sliced watermelon and a cup of taeng mo pan. Even when the same watermelon is used, the preparation and the amount of drink differ.
steps: Cut whole watermelon into bite-size pieces and pick out the seeds as you eat.
When you want to eat on your trip right away, you can pick cut watermelon in a pack too.
If you order taeng mo pan, ask before the drink is made whether the sweetness can be reduced.
watermelon.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a watermelon looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

papaya.name: Papaya
papaya.intro: If you have had som tam in Thailand, try ripe papaya too. Unlike the green papaya used in som tam, the ripe flesh is eaten soft and sweet. Cut it in half, scoop out the black seeds and eat the flesh. When you choose cut fruit, look for ripe papaya.
papaya.taste: Ripe papaya is a fruit where you enjoy the soft flesh. Unripe papaya is also used as an ingredient in dishes, so the texture is different from eating it as fruit.
papaya.why: It is a familiar fruit through som tam, the green papaya salad. In Thailand you can learn about both ways of eating ripe fruit and ways of using unripe fruit in food.
papaya.buying: Choose after telling apart ripe papaya to eat as fruit from green papaya for cooking. Whole fruit and prepared packs may be sold in different price units.
steps: Wash a ripe papaya and cut it in half.
Scoop out the black seeds in the middle, peel the rind and eat the flesh.
Green papaya and ripe papaya are eaten differently, so pick the one to eat right away.
papaya.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a papaya looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

tamarind.name: Sweet Tamarind
tamarind.availability: Timing varies by growing region and variety
tamarind.intro: Try sweet tamarind, which comes in a brown pod. Crack the shell and pull the fibers off the flesh and you can eat the soft inside. If you have only known tamarind as an ingredient in the tangy sauce of Pad Thai, meet sweet tamarind eaten as fruit.
tamarind.taste: Sweet tamarind is a fruit you eat soft and sweet. Remove the hard seed and fibers in the middle and eat the flesh.
tamarind.why: Apart from the tamarind that gives dishes their sourness, there are varieties enjoyed as a sweet fruit. Sweet tamarind of Phetchabun is introduced as a regional GI fruit.
tamarind.buying: Tell apart fresh pods from packaged products with the seeds removed or processed. Even with the same tamarind, the product and the package weight differ.
steps: Crack the shell of the pod and take out the flesh.
Remove the fibers and the hard seed attached to it as you eat the flesh.
A processed product has a different price unit from fresh fruit, so look at the package weight and choose.
tamarind.regional: Phetchabun sweet tamarind: harvest listed for Nov–Apr
tamarind.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what sweet tamarind looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

mandarin.name: Thai Mandarin Orange
mandarin.intro: If you see a citrus fruit with green rind in Thailand, do not assume it is unripe from the color alone. The rind and the taste of a mandarin orange differ by variety. It is easy to peel by hand and eat segment by segment, which makes it a good fruit to share on a trip.
mandarin.taste: You enjoy the sweetness and tartness of citrus together. The taste differs with the variety and ripeness, and the flesh may have seeds.
mandarin.why: Thailand has several mandarin orange varieties. Golden orange of Nan is introduced as a regional GI fruit for its green rind and sweet-tart taste.
mandarin.buying: Compare per-kilogram prices that carry a variety and a size grade among the same grades. Besides the color of the rind, you can choose a fruit to eat right away together with the seller.
steps: Peel the rind and separate the segments to eat.
If the variety has seeds, remove them as you eat.
Look separately at products sold as juice and the per-kilogram price of whole fruit.
mandarin.regional: Nan golden orange: harvest listed for Nov–Dec
mandarin.photoCaption: This is a reference photo showing what a Thai mandarin orange looks like. It is not limited to photos of the Thai growing regions or varieties described in the text.

marian-plum.name: Marian Plum (Mayongchid)
marian-plum.availability: Harvest listed for a regional fruit
marian-plum.intro: If you see a small, yellowish fruit that looks like a little mango in Thailand, ask whether it is mayongchid. It is a fruit of the plum mango group, and mayongchid of Nakhon Nayok is introduced as a regional GI fruit. If you want to try a fruit different from a big mango, look for it in winter and early spring.
marian-plum.taste: Nakhon Nayok mayongchid is introduced as having both sweetness and tartness and crunchy flesh. Remove the seed in the middle and eat.
marian-plum.why: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces mayongchid of Nakhon Nayok as a regional GI fruit. You can learn about a small fruit that looks like a mango together with its growing region.
marian-plum.buying: Even among similar plum mango fruit, the variety and the name differ. Say you are looking for mayongchid, and it helps to get the actual variety and price from the seller.
steps: Wash the fruit you bought and cut it into bite-size pieces.
Remove the seed in the middle and eat the flesh.
There may be other varieties with names similar to mayongchid, so show the name of the fruit you want to buy.
