meta./en-us/food/cities/chiang-mai/: Chiang Mai food guide to Northern Thai dishes: khao soi curry noodles, herb-scented sai ua sausage and tomato dip nam prik ong with sticky rice, plus khantoke dining and tips on longan and lychee.
meta./en-us/food/cities/phuket/: Phuket food guide to local noodles and sweets beyond grilled seafood: thick-noodle mi hokkien, thin rice noodle mi hun and the ice and jelly dessert o-aew, shaped by Chinese and Malay food culture.
meta./en-us/food/cities/ayutthaya/: Ayutthaya food guide to boat noodles, grilled river prawns and roti sai mai, thin roti wrapped around spun sugar, plus river food culture, prawn pricing by size and unit, and fruit buying tips.
meta./en-us/food/cities/khon-kaen/: Khon Kaen food guide to Isan dishes: som tam and larb with sticky rice, fermented sausage sai krok Isan and freshwater fish curry au pla, plus how to ask about pla ra and tell ripe papaya from green.
meta./en-us/food/cities/hat-yai/: Hat Yai food guide to Hat Yai fried chicken with fried shallots and sticky rice and the herbal pork rib soup bak kut teh, plus Songkhla's Chinese and Muslim food culture and halal cautions.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/pad-thai/: Pad Thai is Thailand's best-known stir-fried noodle dish, with rice noodles, egg, tofu and a sweet and tangy tamarind sauce. Learn how it tastes, how to add lime and what to ask about shrimp.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/tom-yum-kung/: Tom Yum Goong is Thailand's hot and sour shrimp soup scented with lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaves. Learn how clear and rich versions differ and what the 2024 UNESCO listing means.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/green-curry/: Thai green curry is a fragrant coconut milk curry with green curry paste, meat and vegetables, eaten with rice or roti. Learn how spicy it is, how to ask about heat and what vegetarians should check.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/massaman/: Massaman curry is a rich Thai curry flavored with cinnamon, cardamom and clove, eaten slowly with rice. Learn how it differs from green curry, why mild still has heat and why halal needs a check.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/mango-sticky-rice/: Mango sticky rice is a Thai dessert of ripe mango with sticky rice flavored with coconut milk. Learn why it counts as a sweet dessert, how to taste mango and rice together and why mango varies.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/khao-soi/: Khao soi is a Northern Thai dish of egg noodles in coconut curry broth topped with crispy fried noodles. Learn why it is famous in Chiang Mai yet eaten across the North, plus chicken or beef.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/sai-ua/: Sai ua is a Northern Thai grilled sausage of pork with chilies, garlic and herbs, a good Chiang Mai pick for a fragrant meat dish. Learn how to start with a small piece and eat it with sticky rice.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/nam-prik-ong/: Nam prik ong is a Northern Thai dipping sauce of tomatoes, ground pork and chilies, eaten with vegetables and sticky rice. Learn why a tomato sauce is not vegetarian and how it pairs with sai ua.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/mi-hokkien/: Mi hokkien is a Phuket dish of thick yellow noodles stir-fried over high heat with seafood and sauce, shaped by Chinese food culture. Learn how it differs from mi hun and what to ask about seafood.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/mi-hun/: Mi hun is a Phuket noodle dish known for thin rice noodles served with pork rib broth, also called mi hun bar chang. Learn how it differs from mi hokkien and what to ask if you avoid pork.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/o-aew/: O-aew is a Phuket dessert of jelly, sweet syrup and toppings over ice, a cold break in Old Phuket Town on a hot day. Learn how to scoop ice and jelly together and what to ask about toppings.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/river-prawns/: Grilled river prawns are a well-known Ayutthaya dish to share, peeled by hand and eaten with rice. Learn how to ask whether the price is per prawn or by weight and why the name does not prove origin.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/boat-noodles/: Boat noodles are a well-known Ayutthaya dish of noodles and meat in broth, a good lunch between sights at the ruins. Learn how to choose noodles, meat and bowl size, and how to ask about offal.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/roti-sai-mai/: Roti sai mai is an Ayutthaya snack of thin roti wrapped around spun sugar, tied to the Muslim community's snack culture. Learn how to wrap it, adjust sweetness and spot the green pandan kind.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/som-tam/: Som tam is a signature Isan papaya salad of shredded unripe papaya pounded with chilies and a sour dressing, best with sticky rice. Learn how to ask about pla ra, a fermented fish seasoning.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/larb/: Larb is an Isan meat salad of minced meat with herbs, lime and toasted rice powder, eaten with sticky rice. Some versions use raw meat, so order it cooked, as Thailand's tourism authority advises.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/sai-krok-isan/: Sai krok Isan is an Isan sausage of pork fermented with rice and garlic, savory with a tang from fermentation. Learn how it differs from sai ua, how to taste the sourness and eat the raw chilies.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/au-pla/: Au pla is a local dish of Khon Kaen in Isan, a spicy and salty freshwater fish curry. Learn how it differs from som tam and larb, how to ask which fish is used and watch for bones.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/hat-yai-chicken/: Hat Yai fried chicken is the signature dish of Hat Yai, crispy chicken seasoned with garlic, coriander root and white pepper, served with fried shallots and sticky rice. Learn how to order it.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/bak-kut-teh/: Bak kut teh is a Chinese-style dish of pork ribs simmered with herbs and spices, found in the Songkhla area. Learn why it is not a Hat Yai original and what to know if you avoid pork.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/roti/: Thai roti is a street snack of thin griddled dough with condensed milk or chocolate, with banana or egg options. Learn how it differs from roti sai mai and what to ask if you cannot eat egg or milk.
meta./en-us/food/dishes/watermelon-shake/: The Thai watermelon shake, taeng mo pan, is watermelon blended with water and ice, a cold street drink for hot days. Learn how it differs from plain juice and how to ask for less sugar or syrup.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/mango/: Thai mango has a main harvest from March to May, with varieties like nam dok mai and maha chanok known for soft, fragrant flesh. Learn about Phitsanulok's Mar–Jun harvest and crisp green mango.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/durian/: Thai durian has a main harvest from April to August, with creamy yellow flesh that is sweet and rich. Learn about monthong, chanee and kan yao, Sisaket durian and why to start with a small portion.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/mangosteen/: Thai mangosteen has a main harvest from April to August, with a purple rind that opens to sweet-tart white segments. Learn about Khao Khiriwong's Jul–Dec harvest and Bangkok's 40–60 baht per kg.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/rambutan/: Thai rambutan has a listed harvest of April to August, with sweet, juicy white flesh inside a spiny red rind. Learn about Na San's Rong Rian rambutan in Jul–Aug and Bangkok's 50–60 baht per kg.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/longan/: Thai longan has a main harvest from June to August, a Northern fruit with translucent flesh and a black seed. Learn about Lamphun's Biao Kiao longan in Jul–Sep and Bangkok's 50–60 baht per kg.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/lychee/: Thai lychee has a listed harvest of April to June, with fragrant, juicy white flesh under a red rind. Learn about Hong Huai and Chakkraphat varieties and Samut Songkhram's Kom lychee in Apr–May.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/longkong/: Thai longkong has a listed harvest of May to September, with sweet-tart translucent segments in bunches. Learn how it differs from longan, Tanyong Mat longkong and Bangkok's 40–50 baht per kg price.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/mandarin/: Thai mandarin oranges have a main harvest from October to February, and green rind does not always mean unripe. Learn about Nan's golden orange in Nov–Dec and Bangkok's 60–65 baht per kg.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/pomelo/: Thai pomelo has a main harvest from October to December, a large citrus fruit with a thick rind and juicy granules. Learn about khao nam phueng and thong dee and how to buy prepared packs.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/pineapple/: Thai pineapple has a main harvest from April to July, and sweetness and firmness change by variety and region. Learn about Trat's Si Thong pineapple and Bangkok's 30–32 baht per kg price.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/banana/: Thai bananas come year-round in many varieties, and Kamphaeng Phet's Kluai Khai banana is a regional GI fruit. Learn why they are sold by the bunch and Bangkok's 40–50 baht price for a Nam Wa bunch.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/coconut/: Thai young coconut is a year-round fruit you open to drink the water, then scoop out the soft flesh. Learn about fragrant nam hom, Ban Phaeo's GI coconut and how it differs from a bottled drink.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/papaya/: Thai papaya is a year-round fruit, and unlike the green papaya in som tam, ripe flesh is soft and sweet. Learn how to halve, seed and peel it, how to pick ripe fruit and Bangkok's 40–60 baht per kg.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/watermelon/: Thai watermelon is a year-round fruit to eat sliced or as taeng mo pan, the watermelon shake blended with ice. Learn how kg, sliced and cup prices differ, with Bangkok's 25–30 baht per kg listing.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/tamarind/: Thai sweet tamarind has a main harvest listed from late December to February, with soft sweet flesh in a brown pod. Learn how it differs from sour tamarind and Phetchabun's Nov–Apr harvest.
meta./en-us/food/fruits/marian-plum/: Marian plum, called mayongchid in Thai, is a small yellowish fruit of the plum mango group, and Nakhon Nayok's mayongchid is a regional GI fruit harvested Jan–Mar. Learn its sweet-tart, crunchy bite.
